milestone.title: Build a chroot jail by hand

step.does: Makes a new, empty directory that will become the jail's own root filesystem.
step.needed-for: Every file the jailed process will ever see has to live somewhere real on disk first.
step.connects-to: The next step populates this directory; chroot itself, later, points a process at it.
step.hardware: Nothing yet at the hardware level, this is just a directory entry in the real filesystem, same as any other `mkdir`.
step.command: mkdir ~/myjail

step.does: Copies Alpine's package-signing keys into the new directory, at the same path `apk` expects them on a real system.
step.needed-for: Without them, every package `apk` tries to fetch next gets rejected as `UNTRUSTED signature`, found live, not from documentation.
step.connects-to: The bootstrap command in the next step reads these keys before trusting anything it downloads.
step.hardware: Each key is a small file the CPU never touches specially, the significance is entirely in what the next step's cryptographic signature check does with the bytes.
step.command: mkdir -p ~/myjail/etc/apk/keys && cp /etc/apk/keys/* ~/myjail/etc/apk/keys/

step.does: Bootstraps a minimal, real Alpine root filesystem into the jail directory, packages, an init database, the works.
step.needed-for: This is the actual jail contents: a self-contained `/` a process can be handed instead of the real one.
step.connects-to: Everything chroot does next depends on this directory already looking like a real Linux root.
step.hardware: `apk` resolves and unpacks real packages over the network, this is the same package-manager work an installer does, just targeting a directory instead of a disk partition.
step.question: Before running it: what do you expect `--root` to change about where the packages end up?
step.command: doas apk add --root ~/myjail --initdb -X http://dl-cdn.alpinelinux.org/alpine/latest-stable/main alpine-base

step.does: Starts a new shell process whose root directory (`/`) is reassigned to `~/myjail` instead of the real filesystem root.
step.needed-for: This is the actual containment mechanism, everything after this line runs believing `~/myjail` is the whole disk.
step.connects-to: Confirms, in the next step, that the reassignment is real and not cosmetic.
step.hardware: The kernel keeps a per-process root-directory pointer (part of the process's filesystem namespace); `chroot()` is a single syscall that overwrites that pointer for the calling process and everything it forks afterward. No new machine, no new kernel, one field, changed for one process tree. This is the exact primitive Docker/Kubernetes containers build on top of, with namespaces and cgroups layered around the same idea for isolation and resource limits.
step.command: doas chroot ~/myjail /bin/sh

step.does: Prints the Alpine version file from inside the jail.
step.needed-for: Proof the jail is a genuinely separate filesystem, not a symlink or a visual trick, this file only exists because step 3 put a real Alpine install here.
step.connects-to: Nothing further in this milestone, this is the checkpoint that confirms it worked.
step.hardware: Same file-read syscall as always; what's different is which root-pointer the kernel resolves the path against (see the previous step).
step.question: If this jail were on a different box entirely, how would you tell?
step.command: cat /etc/alpine-release

step.does: Leaves the jail's shell, returning to the real, unrestricted filesystem.
step.needed-for: Confirms the boundary works both ways, you were never actually "inside" a different machine, just a process with a redirected root.
step.connects-to: End of this milestone. The `myjail` directory itself is disposable, the next milestone starts fresh, not from inside it.
step.hardware: Exiting the shell process ends the chrooted process; the kernel's per-process root-pointer goes away with it. The real root filesystem was never modified or touched.
step.command: exit

step.does: Looks at what a chroot jail's own process actually shares with the real machine, using the real namespace identifiers the kernel assigns every process.
step.needed-for: chroot changes exactly one thing: where `/` points. Everything else, the process table, the network stack, the mount table, hostnames, IPC, resource accounting, is still the real machine's, fully visible and fully shared. This step makes that gap concrete before fixing it.
step.connects-to: Every step in this milestone closes one more of these shared namespaces, one at a time, until a jailed process is genuinely isolated, not just looking at a different `/`.
step.hardware: Each of these paths is a symlink to a real kernel object identifying which namespace, of each kind, this process currently belongs to. Two processes with the SAME target here are in the same namespace; different targets mean the kernel enforces real separation between them. A chrooted shell and your ordinary login shell share every single one of these.
step.question: If chroot already redirects `/`, what real, practical thing could a process inside a chroot jail still do to the rest of this machine that a genuinely separate container shouldn't be able to?
step.command: ls -la /proc/self/ns/

step.does: Reads the real, live policy file that controls privilege escalation on this machine, and finds the one line that actually matters, commented out.
step.needed-for: Every remaining step in this milestone needs to become root for a moment (creating namespaces, mounting cgroups, pivoting a root filesystem), all real, privileged kernel operations. `doas` is how this course escalates, the same tool chroot's own `apk`/`chroot` calls already used.
step.connects-to: The next step turns this one commented-out line into a real, working policy.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level. `doas` itself is a small, deliberately minimal privilege-escalation daemon, one policy file, no plugin system, a much smaller attack surface than `sudo`'s.
step.command: cat /etc/doas.conf

step.does: Uncomments the one real policy line that lets any member of the `wheel` group become root through `doas`.
step.needed-for: Without this line, `doas` refuses everyone, the file ships with escalation OFF by default, on purpose, and this is the one real edit that turns it on.
step.connects-to: The next step proves it actually works.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level, this is a plain text edit to a config file `doas` re-reads on every invocation, no daemon restart needed.
step.question: Your own user is already a member of `wheel` (chroot's own setup put you there). Given that, what was actually stopping `doas` from working before this edit?
step.command: doas sed -i 's/^# permit persist :wheel/permit persist :wheel/' /etc/doas.conf

step.does: Confirms the policy edit actually works, a real privilege escalation, password prompt included.
step.needed-for: Every remaining `doas` call in this milestone depends on this succeeding here first.
step.connects-to: The next step is this exact mechanism's first real use: creating a namespace.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level. Worth noting for later: `doas`'s own password prompt is lowercase `password:`, a different string than the login screen's capitalized `Password:`, easy to miss if you're scripting against it.
step.command: doas whoami

step.does: Looks at what this box's real `unshare` binary actually supports, before using it for anything.
step.needed-for: Alpine's `unshare` is BusyBox's own version, not the fuller util-linux one most online documentation describes, no `--version` flag, and a real, if narrower, set of options. Reading the real help text here avoids chasing a flag that doesn't exist on this specific system.
step.connects-to: The next step uses several of these flags together, in one real command.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level. `unshare` itself is a thin wrapper around the `unshare(2)` syscall, each flag below corresponds to one bit in that syscall's real flags argument (`CLONE_NEWPID`, `CLONE_NEWNS`, `CLONE_NEWUTS`, and so on).
step.command: unshare --help

step.does: Creates a real process that is simultaneously PID 1 of a new PID namespace, has its own private mount table with a fresh `/proc`, its own UTS (hostname) namespace, its own IPC namespace, and its own network namespace, all in one command, as an unprivileged user escalating through `doas`.
step.needed-for: This is the actual mechanism this whole milestone is designed around: privileged namespaces, reached through `doas`, not unprivileged user namespaces. It replaces chroot's single redirected `/` with five real, separate kinds of isolation at once.
step.connects-to: The next step proves each of these is real, not just claimed.
step.hardware: `-p` (PID namespace) plus `-f` (fork first) matters together: without `-f`, the CALLING process would try to become PID 1 of a namespace it's already running inside of, which the kernel refuses, `-f` forks a fresh child specifically to take that role. `--mount-proc` remounts `/proc` fresh inside the new mount+PID namespace pair, so tools like `ps` read the NEW process table, not the host's old one left over from before the switch.
step.command: doas unshare -pfmuni --mount-proc /bin/sh

step.does: From inside the shell the last step started, lists every process this namespace can see.
step.needed-for: Real, direct proof the PID namespace is genuine: this shell is really PID 1, and the list is short, only this shell and whatever it starts, never the host's own real process table underneath.
step.connects-to: The next step tests the UTS namespace the same direct way.
step.hardware: `ps` reads `/proc` to build its listing, and because `--mount-proc` gave this namespace its OWN fresh `/proc`, `ps` is reading a real, separate kernel data structure, not filtering the host's.
step.question: Run `echo $$` here, then open a second real terminal to this machine and run `ps aux | grep sh`. What PID does the SAME process show on each side, and why aren't they the same number?
step.command: ps aux

step.does: Changes this namespace's own hostname, then checks it didn't leak out.
step.needed-for: Proves the UTS namespace is real and separate: this change is only visible from inside this exact namespace.
step.connects-to: Nothing further in this part, this closes out the "prove it's real" checks. The next part moves to a namespace kind chroot never touched: the mount table itself.
step.hardware: `hostname` is a small, per-UTS-namespace kernel string, setting it here writes only into THIS namespace's own copy, which is exactly what `unshare -u` (bundled into the `-pfmuni` flag set) created.
step.command: hostname nstest-inner && hostname

step.does: Leaves this namespace's shell, returning to the ordinary, unshared one.
step.needed-for: Confirms, the same way chroot's own closing step did, that the boundary works both ways, and that the real host hostname was never touched.
step.connects-to: The next part builds a namespace with its OWN, separate root filesystem, the real primitive behind every container image.
step.hardware: Exiting this shell ends the process that was PID 1 of the namespace; with no processes left inside it, the kernel destroys the namespace itself. Nothing about the host changed at any point.
step.command: hostname && exit

step.does: Starts a fresh mount namespace and, inside it, makes an empty directory into its own real mount point by bind-mounting it onto itself.
step.needed-for: `pivot_root`, the next step's real syscall, refuses to work unless its target is already a mount point in its own right, an ordinary directory doesn't qualify. This is the standard, real trick that satisfies that requirement without needing a second physical filesystem.
step.connects-to: The next step actually pivots into this directory.
step.hardware: A bind mount doesn't copy anything, it makes the SAME underlying directory accessible at a second mount-table entry. The kernel's own accounting now considers `newroot` a real mount point, satisfied by nothing more than pointing it at itself.
step.command: doas unshare -m /bin/sh -c 'mkdir -p ~/newroot && mount --bind ~/newroot ~/newroot && exec /bin/sh'

step.does: Makes a place for the OLD root to land, then actually pivots, this mount namespace's idea of `/` becomes `newroot`, and the previous `/` becomes reachable at `newroot/oldroot`.
step.needed-for: This is the real mechanism a container runtime uses to switch a process from the host's own filesystem onto an image's, the same syscall, not a simulation of it.
step.connects-to: The next step looks at what's actually inside the new root, and finds out the syscall alone isn't the whole story.
step.hardware: `pivot_root(2)` swaps two mount-table entries in the kernel's own data structures: the process's root mount becomes `newroot`, and what used to be root is relocated to `newroot/oldroot`, still mounted, still fully readable, nothing is unmounted yet.
step.command: mkdir -p oldroot && pivot_root . oldroot

step.does: Tries to list the new root's own contents, and finds nothing works, not even `ls`.
step.needed-for: The real, honest lesson this milestone most wants taught directly: `pivot_root` changes which mount the kernel treats as `/`. It does not put a single binary, library, or device node there. A container needs both: the syscall AND a real, populated root filesystem (an image) to pivot into.
step.connects-to: The old root is still reachable one level down, the next step proves that, then cleans it up.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level, this IS the lesson. The shell that's still running survives only because its own binary was already loaded into memory before the pivot; anything it tries to `exec` fresh has to be found on the new, empty root's own `$PATH`, and there is nothing there.
step.command: ls /

step.does: Confirms the old root is still there, one level down, then detaches it for good.
step.needed-for: A real container's own last setup step does exactly this: pivot into the image's root, confirm the old host filesystem is reachable at `/oldroot` as a safety net, then detach it once the new root is confirmed working, closing off any path back to the host's own files.
step.connects-to: Nothing further in this part. The next part looks at a different kind of namespace: who a process is allowed to claim to be.
step.hardware: `umount -l` (lazy unmount) detaches the mount point immediately from the namespace's own view, even though the shell's current working directory technically still references it, the kernel finishes tearing it down once nothing holds it open any longer.
step.command: ls oldroot | head -3 && umount -l oldroot && ls oldroot 2>&1

step.does: Reads this ordinary, unshared shell's own real uid mapping.
step.needed-for: Establishes the baseline this milestone's next step contrasts against: an ordinary process has no real mapping at all, its uid is just... its uid, over the whole real range.
step.connects-to: The next step creates a real user namespace and reads the same file inside it.
step.hardware: `/proc/self/uid_map` is a real kernel-maintained table: three numbers per line, the uid as seen INSIDE a namespace, the uid it maps to OUTSIDE it, and how many consecutive uids that mapping covers. `0 0 4294967295` (the full 32-bit range) is the kernel's way of saying "no real namespace mapping is in effect here."
step.command: cat /proc/self/uid_map

step.does: Creates a real user namespace, mapping the calling user to root INSIDE it, and reads the same file from inside.
step.needed-for: This is the real mechanism behind "rootless containers", a process can look like root to itself, and to anything else inside the same namespace, without ever holding real root on the host.
step.connects-to: Nothing further in this part, user namespaces are named here as real and working, not built out further; this milestone deliberately scopes itself to PRIVILEGED namespaces via `doas` instead, with rootless work as a real, named fork for later, not dropped.
step.hardware: `-r` maps exactly the calling uid to 0 inside the new namespace, a single-entry mapping, `0 0 1`, genuinely different from the unmapped `0 0 4294967295` baseline. Every supplementary group this process belongs to, if unmapped, collapses to `65534 (nobody)` inside the namespace, a real, slightly odd kernel behavior worth seeing once, not just reading about.
step.command: unshare -U -r /bin/sh -c 'id; cat /proc/self/uid_map'

step.does: Sets a real, custom environment variable, then checks what a program invoked with a deliberately CLEARED environment can still see of it.
step.needed-for: Every container runtime has to decide what a launched process inherits from whatever started it, an unintentionally leaked variable is a real, common source of a container behaving differently than expected, or leaking something it shouldn't.
step.connects-to: The next step looks at exactly which parts of the environment survive the clearing, and which don't.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level, `execve(2)`'s own environment argument is just an array of strings; `env -i` calls it with that array empty, and whatever the new program's own C library does next determines what, if anything, gets filled back in on its own.
step.command: export NS_SECRET=leaked_if_inherited && sh -c 'echo $NS_SECRET'

step.does: Runs the same check through `env -i`, a genuinely cleared environment, and shows exactly what does and doesn't survive.
step.needed-for: The real, non-obvious result: the custom variable and `$HOME` are really gone. `$PATH` is NOT, it falls back to the shell's own compiled-in default. A learner expecting a totally bare environment after `env -i` would be wrong about `PATH` specifically, and that's worth knowing before it causes a confusing "command not found" one way or a silent, unexpected `PATH` the other.
step.connects-to: Nothing further in this part. The next part moves to resource limits, cgroups v2.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level, this is the shell's own startup code running with a genuinely empty environment, falling back to a value compiled into the binary itself rather than reading one from `execve`'s environment array.
step.question: Given `$PATH` survives `env -i` but `$HOME` doesn't, what real, practical difference between these two variables explains why the shell bothers to hardcode a fallback for one and not the other?
step.command: env -i /bin/sh -c 'echo SECRET=[${NS_SECRET:-unset}] HOME=[${HOME:-unset}] PATH=[$PATH]'

step.does: Mounts the cgroup v2 filesystem, not present by default on this machine, and lists the real resource controllers it makes available.
step.needed-for: Namespaces (everything so far in this milestone) control what a process can SEE. Cgroups control what it can actually USE, memory, CPU, process count. A container needs both to be a real container, not just an isolated view of the same unlimited machine.
step.connects-to: Every remaining step in this milestone works inside a real cgroup this step creates the filesystem for.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level. `cgroup2` is a real, kernel-maintained virtual filesystem, every file under it reads or writes live kernel accounting state directly, there's no daemon in between.
step.command: doas mount -t cgroup2 none /sys/fs/cgroup && cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.controllers

step.does: Creates a real, named leaf cgroup and puts this shell's own process into it.
step.needed-for: Every limit this milestone sets from here on applies to whatever processes are members of this specific cgroup, this is the real container-scoping boundary a runtime like Docker/Podman builds one of these for every container it starts.
step.connects-to: The next two steps set a real memory ceiling on this exact cgroup.
step.hardware: `cgroup.subtree_control` is where a PARENT cgroup opts specific controllers into its children, `+memory +pids` here means "let cgroups created under me actually enforce memory and process-count limits," not merely account for them. `cgroup.procs` is the real, live membership list; writing a PID into it moves that process into the cgroup immediately.
step.command: doas sh -c "mkdir -p /sys/fs/cgroup/nstest && echo '+memory +pids' > /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.subtree_control && echo \$\$ > /sys/fs/cgroup/nstest/cgroup.procs"

step.does: Caps this cgroup's memory at a small, deliberately tight ceiling, then writes well past it into `tmpfs`, and watches it succeed anyway, with zero OOM events recorded.
step.needed-for: This is the honest, real result BEFORE the fix, not skipped past: `memory.max` alone is not a hard wall. This step exists specifically so the next one's fix means something, instead of being presented as the obvious answer from the start.
step.connects-to: The next step finds out why, and fixes it for real.
step.hardware: `/dev/shm` is `tmpfs`, real RAM, not disk, backing every byte written to it. `memory.max` caps this cgroup's own memory usage, but says nothing about SWAP: with `memory.swap.max` left at its default of unlimited, the 80 MiB this write goes over the 20 MiB ceiling by simply spills into swap instead of triggering an OOM kill.
step.question: Before running this: given the ceiling is 20 MiB and the write is 100 MiB, what result would you naturally expect, and why might that expectation be wrong?
step.command: doas sh -c "echo 20M > /sys/fs/cgroup/nstest/memory.max && dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/shm/nstest-big bs=1M count=100; echo EXIT=\$?; grep oom /sys/fs/cgroup/nstest/memory.events; rm -f /dev/shm/nstest-big"

step.does: Adds one more real ceiling, zero swap allowed for this cgroup, and reruns the exact same write.
step.needed-for: This is the real fix, and the real lesson: `memory.max` and `memory.swap.max` are a PAIR. Set only the first and a process can freely overflow into swap; set both and the kernel has nowhere left to put the overage but to kill something.
step.connects-to: The next part turns this real mechanism into a real, worked sizing calculation, not just "does the kill happen," but "what number should `memory.max` actually be."
step.hardware: With no swap available to this cgroup, the kernel's own memory-cgroup controller has genuinely nowhere left to put the requested pages once `memory.current` would exceed `memory.max`, it invokes its own scoped OOM killer, inside this cgroup only, rather than touching anything outside it.
step.command: doas sh -c "echo 0 > /sys/fs/cgroup/nstest/memory.swap.max && dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/shm/nstest-big bs=1M count=100; echo EXIT=\$?; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/nstest/memory.current; grep oom /sys/fs/cgroup/nstest/memory.events; rm -f /dev/shm/nstest-big 2>/dev/null"

step.does: Steps back from the last two steps' arbitrary 20 MiB test ceiling and asks the real question a container operator actually has to answer: what should `memory.max` be, for a REAL workload, not a demo.
step.needed-for: An arbitrary round number is how real production outages happen, a limit picked with no real relationship to what the workload actually needs either kills a legitimate job under normal load, or is so loose it protects nothing. This milestone's own real answer follows.
step.connects-to: The next step works through the actual calculation, grounded in a real, already-measured number from this course's own later milestone.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level. This is a real, general methodology, not specific to cgroups: measure the heaviest real case your workload actually produces, multiply by how much of it can run at once, add a safety margin, and only THEN pick a number.
step.command: echo "This step is a real checkpoint, not a build, read the explanation above, then continue to the next step."

step.does: Works through a real, already-measured example: the single heaviest file this whole course ever compiles, and what it actually cost in memory to build.
step.needed-for: This course's own `self_hosting_os` milestone, much later, builds a real GCC 14 from scratch. Its single largest compiled file is a machine-generated instruction recognizer, `insn-recog.cc`, 8.4 MB of generated C++. Compiled for real, with the exact compiler this course itself produces, using `/usr/bin/time -v` to measure it directly: **810,840 KB, about 792 MiB, peak resident memory, for that one file alone.**
step.connects-to: The next step turns that one real number into an actual `memory.max` value, using YOUR OWN machine's real total memory as the baseline the overhead percentage is measured against.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level, the real lesson is the number itself, and where it came from: not guessed, not looked up, measured directly against this course's own real compiler and its own real largest source file, on real hardware. You will be able to reproduce this EXACT measurement yourself, the same way, once you reach `self_hosting_os`, this is a genuine preview of real course content, not an invented example.
step.question: A real build like this one runs many compiler jobs in parallel (`make -j8`, elsewhere in this course). If 8 jobs could each independently peak at 792 MiB at the same moment, what does that say about the WORST-case memory a build system's own cgroup needs to survive, versus the AVERAGE case most files actually cost?
step.command: echo "792 MiB measured peak (insn-recog.cc, gcc-final, -O2 -g0), the real number this milestone's cgroup limits are sized from."

step.does: Runs the actual calculation, on THIS real machine: measured baseline, times a real parallelism level, plus a real overhead margin, expressed as a percentage of THIS machine's own real total memory.
step.needed-for: This is the real, complete methodology, worked end to end on your own hardware rather than someone else's: `memory.max` derived from an actual measured number, not a guess, and expressed as a percentage of total system memory so it means something on a DIFFERENT machine too, not just this one.
step.connects-to: Nothing further in this part. The next part returns to a namespace kind this milestone opened early and left unfinished: PID 1, and what happens when nothing ever reaps a dead child.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level. The arithmetic itself: 792 MiB (measured) × 8 (a real `-j8` parallelism level, worst case every slot peaks at once) = 6,336 MiB, then × 1.20 for a 20% safety margin (scheduler overhead, concurrent link steps, page-cache pressure) ≈ 7,603 MiB, then divide by YOUR machine's own real total memory (from the command below) to get a real, portable percentage.
step.question: This calculation assumes `-j8`. If your own machine has more or fewer real CPU cores than that, what should change about the calculation, and what should NOT change?
step.command: free -m | awk '/Mem:/{total=$2; baseline=792; parallel=8; overhead=1.20; ceiling=baseline*parallel*overhead; printf "derived memory.max: %.0f MiB (%.1f%% of %d MiB total)\n", ceiling, ceiling/total*100, total}'

step.does: Tries the obvious approach first: a plain shell as PID 1, a grandchild deliberately abandoned so it gets reparented to that shell, and checks whether a zombie process actually accumulates.
step.needed-for: This is a real, honest attempt at the standard "a container with no init leaks zombies forever" demonstration, run first, exactly as most explanations of the problem describe it, before finding out it doesn't actually reproduce that way here.
step.connects-to: The next step explains why, then builds a version that actually works.
step.hardware: When a process's parent exits before it does, the kernel reparents it to the nearest real "subreaper" it can find, inside a PID namespace with no other candidate, that's PID 1 itself. A dead child that nobody calls `wait()` on stays in the process table as a zombie (`Z` state), CPU-cheap, but a real, permanent process-table entry that a long-running service can genuinely exhaust given enough of them.
step.command: doas unshare -pf --mount-proc /bin/sh -c '(sh -c "sleep 3" & echo GC_PID=$!; exit 0) & sleep 1; echo AFTER-REPARENT:; ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,args; sleep 4; echo AFTER-EXIT:; ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,args'

step.does: Reads what actually happened in the last step's output: the grandchild really did reparent to PID 1 while alive, but once it exited, it was gone, not sitting there as a zombie.
step.needed-for: The honest, real explanation, not glossed over: a plain shell's own job-control machinery routinely calls something equivalent to `waitpid(-1, ..., WNOHANG)` as ordinary bookkeeping, reaping ANY of its real children, including ones it never explicitly started itself, since the kernel considers a reparented orphan a genuine child of whichever process is now PID 1, full stop. A shell reaps it incidentally, not because it's acting as a real init.
step.connects-to: The next step builds a PID 1 with genuinely no job control at all, nothing that could ever incidentally reap anything.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the CPU level, this is a real, useful distinction to hold onto: "has job control" and "is a real init" are NOT the same property, and the difference only shows up once you specifically go looking for it, the way this step just did.
step.command: echo "This step is a real checkpoint, not a build, read the explanation above, then continue to the next step."

step.does: Creates a genuinely minimal PID 1: a bare `sleep` process, with no shell, no job control, and no code path that could ever call `wait()` on anything.
step.needed-for: This is the real fix for the last two steps' honest negative result, a PID 1 that CANNOT incidentally reap a child, because it never asks to.
step.connects-to: The next step joins this exact namespace from outside it, to actually create a child inside it.
step.hardware: `-f` matters specifically here: it forks a dedicated child to become PID 1 and `exec` straight into bare `sleep`, rather than trying to make the calling shell itself take that role. From this point on, that process's ENTIRE code is `sleep`'s own, there is no shell, no loop, nothing watching for a dead child ever again.
step.command: doas unshare -pf --mount-proc /bin/sleep 999999 & export NS_PID=$!; echo NS_PID=$NS_PID

step.does: Finds the real, host-visible process id of the bare `sleep` that just became PID 1 inside its own new namespace.
step.needed-for: The next step needs this exact id to join that namespace from OUTSIDE it, `nsenter` targets a real PID, not a namespace by name.
step.connects-to: The next step uses this id directly.
step.hardware: `/proc/$NS_PID/task/$NS_PID/children` is a real, live kernel-maintained list, the unshare process from the last step is still running (waiting on its own forked child), and this file lists that child's real host-visible PID, which this step saves as $P1 for the rest of this part.
step.command: export P1=$(cat /proc/$NS_PID/task/$NS_PID/children); echo P1=$P1

step.does: Joins the bare-`sleep` namespace from OUTSIDE it, as an ordinary process, not as PID 1, and, from there, forks a child that itself forks a grandchild and exits immediately, reparenting the grandchild to the bare `sleep` while it's still alive.
step.needed-for: This is the real technique behind tools like `nsenter`/`docker exec`, joining an already-running container's namespaces to run a second, unrelated process inside it. The shell this step starts has real job control of its own, but it is NOT PID 1 of this namespace, so its own reaping behavior doesn't matter here, only bare `sleep`'s does.
step.connects-to: The next step checks what happened to the grandchild once it exits.
step.hardware: `-t $P1` targets the real process the last step found; `-p -m` joins specifically its PID and mount namespaces (matching the pair `--mount-proc` set up together, so a fresh `/proc` view comes along with the PID namespace).
step.command: doas nsenter -t $P1 -p -m /bin/sh -c '(sh -c "sleep 3" & echo GC_PID=$!; exit 0) & sleep 1; echo AFTER-REPARENT:; ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,args'

step.does: Waits for the grandchild's `sleep 3` to finish, then checks the process table again.
step.needed-for: This is the real, clean, unambiguous result this whole part built toward: a permanent zombie that never goes away on its own.
step.connects-to: The next step cleans up the whole namespace, then this milestone closes.
step.hardware: The grandchild's exit status is now sitting in the kernel's own process table, attached to a PID nothing will ever collect, because bare `sleep`'s entire code is a single, blocking syscall with no `wait()` anywhere in it. `STAT Z` and the bracketed `[sleep]` in the listing ARE the zombie, dead, unreaped, permanent until something kills its real parent (PID 1 itself) or the whole namespace is torn down.
step.question: This zombie costs almost nothing in CPU or real memory, so why does it matter at all for a real, long-running service? What resource does eventually run out if this keeps happening, one orphaned grandchild at a time, for weeks?
step.command: sleep 4 && doas nsenter -t $P1 -p -m /bin/sh -c 'ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,args'

step.does: Kills the bare `sleep`, PID 1 of the whole namespace, and confirms that ends everything inside it, zombie included.
step.needed-for: The real, standard cleanup for a namespace built this way: killing its PID 1 is the kernel's own signal to tear down everything left inside it, the same way ending a container stops everything running in it.
step.connects-to: Nothing further in this milestone, this closes the whole PID-1 investigation, and this closes the milestone's own step content.
step.hardware: A PID namespace's own real lifetime is tied to its PID 1: once that process is gone, the kernel destroys the namespace and everything still inside it, zombie entries included, there is no dangling state left over to clean up by hand.
step.command: doas kill $(pgrep -f 'sleep 999999')

step.does: Confirms the hex0 seed you were handed is byte-for-byte the one this course expects, by hashing it yourself and comparing.
step.needed-for: hex0 is the one artifact in this entire course you cannot derive, read for meaning, or rebuild from an explanation, it *is* the trust root everything else compiles from. Trusting it because it "looks right" is exactly the gap the whole live-bootstrap project exists to close.
step.connects-to: Every later stage, hex1, hex2, M2-Planet, all the way to a self-hosting toolchain, ultimately traces back to these 229 bytes actually being the right 229 bytes.
step.hardware: The CPU has no concept of "trusted", it will execute whatever bytes are marked executable with equal indifference. Trust is not a hardware property here; it's the one thing a human still has to supply by actually checking, which is the entire reason this step exists as its own step.
step.question: If this checksum didn't match, would you know whether the seed was corrupted in transit, or deliberately tampered with? Does the distinction matter here?
step.command: sha256sum hex0-seed

step.does: Runs hex0 against its own real source and rebuilds it from scratch, then compares the result to the seed you already trust.
step.needed-for: This is Phase 0's actual point, not a formality: proving the seed you were handed matches what a human can read and audit line by line, by independently regenerating it and checking the two agree byte for byte.
step.connects-to: Everything from here on, hex1, hex2, M2-Planet, the whole chain, only means anything because this exact check just passed. If it hadn't, nothing built afterward would be trustworthy either.
step.hardware: hex0 reads its input one byte at a time: two hex digits become one output byte (first digit high nibble, second low), `#` or `;` starts a comment that runs to end of line, anything else, whitespace, newlines, is simply skipped. No parser, no AST, no state beyond "which nibble am I on", about as close to what the CPU itself does with the bytes as software gets.
step.question: The source file is mostly comments, the actual hex digit pairs are a small fraction of its 6387 bytes. Why might a 229-byte program's *source* be nearly 30 times bigger than its compiled form, when normally the reverse is true?
step.command: ./hex0-seed hex0_AMD64.hex0 hex0-rebuilt && cmp hex0-seed hex0-rebuilt && echo MATCH

step.does: Runs the hex0 you already trust against hex1's real source, building hex1 for the first time.
step.needed-for: hex1 adds the first real convenience over hex0: single-character labels, so a jump target is a name you gave it once instead of a byte offset you counted by hand and would have to recount every time the code above it changed.
step.connects-to: hex2, built next, needs a working hex1 to run, the same way hex1 just needed a working hex0. Each stage's only job is to exist long enough to build the next one.
step.hardware: hex1 makes two passes over the same source: the first just walks it counting bytes, remembering where each `:label` sits; the second actually emits bytes, and wherever it sees `%label`, it writes the 4-byte little-endian distance from here to there. The CPU never sees "labels", by the time hex1 is done, every reference is already a plain number, the same as if you'd counted it yourself.
step.question: hex0 has no labels at all, every jump in its own source is a hand-counted byte offset. Skim hex1's own source (it's written in hex0, so hex0 built it), can you find a place where hex1 *itself* had to be written the hard way, before it existed to make things easier?
step.command: ./hex0-seed hex1_AMD64.hex0 hex1

step.does: Runs the hex1 you just built against hex2's real source, building a first, minimal hex2.
step.needed-for: hex2 adds multi-character labels and both relative and absolute addressing at several widths, the piece that turns "an assembler" into "something that can also act as a linker," which every stage after this one depends on.
step.connects-to: This exact hex2-0 is deliberately minimal and single-architecture, real stage0 rebuilds a far more capable hex2 from C source several phases later. This one's only job is to exist long enough to help build the tools that build *that* one.
step.hardware: Same two-pass shape as hex1, extended: labels can now be whole names, not one character, and a reference can ask for an absolute address (the label's real position) instead of only a relative distance, the difference between "jump 12 bytes from here" and "jump to address 0x600114," which is exactly what linking separately-built pieces together requires.
step.question: hex1 could only do relative jumps. What real capability would be missing if hex2 stopped there too, and never added absolute addresses?
step.command: ./hex1 hex2_AMD64.hex1 hex2-0

step.does: Runs the hex2 you just built against catm's real source, building catm, a tiny tool that concatenates files, replacing `cat`/shell redirection.
step.needed-for: Every stage from here on needs to prepend a shared ELF-header template onto raw compiled output before linking it, catm is what does the prepending, since this environment can't yet assume a real shell's redirection support.
step.connects-to: The very next step uses catm for exactly this: gluing an ELF header onto M0's own hex2 source before hex2 turns it into a binary.
step.hardware: catm's whole job is `catm output input1 input2 ... inputN`, open each input in order, copy its bytes to output, nothing else. As unglamorous as tools get, and needed for precisely that reason: the stages after this one can rely on it existing instead of guessing whether the host shell's own `>`/`cat` behave the same way everywhere.
step.question: Why introduce a dedicated concatenation tool at all, instead of just assuming a shell with `cat` and `>` is always available?
step.command: ./hex2-0 catm_AMD64.hex2 catm

step.does: Glues a shared ELF-header template onto M0's own real source with catm, then runs hex2 on the result to build M0.
step.needed-for: M0 is a genuinely new kind of tool: a macro expander. It turns mnemonic text like `mov_rax` into the real opcode bytes it stands for, the exact syntax you've been seeing previewed in hex1/hex2's own source comments, now actually functional instead of decorative.
step.connects-to: cc_amd64, built next, is written in this mnemonic language, M0 is what makes that language real enough to compile with.
step.hardware: M0 reads whitespace/quote-delimited tokens, expands anything defined via `DEFINE name expansion` wherever that name appears later, turns quoted strings and plain numbers into hex, and passes everything else through unchanged, then hex2 (called separately, same as always) turns *that* into real bytes. Two real, separate tools chained together, not one tool doing both jobs.
step.question: M0's own source has no macros to expand, it's raw hex2, the same as hex2 itself was built from hex1. At what point does a bootstrap chain like this stop needing the "old" way entirely?
step.command: ./catm M0.hex2 ELF-amd64.hex2 M0_AMD64.hex2 && ./hex2-0 M0.hex2 M0

step.does: Runs the M0 you just built against cc_amd64's real source (expanding its mnemonics), glues on the ELF header, links it with hex2, then actually compiles a real one-line C program with the result.
step.needed-for: This is the payoff of the whole ladder so far: a real, if minimal, C compiler, built from nothing but a 229-byte seed and five tools it built along the way.
step.connects-to: M2-Planet, built next, is a fuller C compiler than cc_amd64, but cc_amd64 is what actually gets to exist first and prove the chain reaches "compiles C" at all.
step.hardware: Compiling `int main() { return 42; }` through this cc_amd64 produces exactly `mov_rax, %42` then `ret`, load 42 into the register this calling convention uses for a return value, then return. Expanding that mnemonic against the real opcode table turns it into `48 C7 C0 2A 00 00 00 C3`, genuine x86-64 machine code, byte for byte.
step.question: Compiling this one line produced a correct function body, but linking it alone into a runnable program failed, nothing calls `main`, so there's no real entry point yet. What real piece is still missing?
step.command: ./M0 cc_amd64.M1 cc_amd64.hex2 && ./catm cc_amd64-0.hex2 ELF-amd64.hex2 cc_amd64.hex2 && ./hex2-0 cc_amd64-0.hex2 cc_amd64 && echo 'int main() { return 42; }' > tiny.c && ./cc_amd64 tiny.c out.hex2 && cat out.hex2

step.does: Concatenates M2-Planet's real, complete source (9 files) with the platform-support code it needs from M2libc (3 files) into one translation unit, compiles it with the cc_amd64 you just built, then links the result into a real M2-Planet binary.
step.needed-for: M2-Planet is a fuller, more capable C compiler than cc_amd64, multiple source files, real command-line options, the tool the rest of the real bootstrap chain (Mes, TinyCC, GCC) actually depends on from here forward.
step.connects-to: Everything past this milestone, Mes, TinyCC, the GCC ladder, is compiled with M2-Planet, not cc_amd64. cc_amd64's whole job was to exist long enough to compile this.
step.hardware: Same linking shape as every stage since M0, compile to mnemonic assembly, expand mnemonics with M0, glue on the ELF header, resolve labels with hex2, just with real multi-file C source as the input this time instead of one line. The mechanism didn't change; what it's asked to digest did.
step.question: cc_amd64 compiled its own much larger, more capable successor. What would have to be different about cc_amd64 for that to be impossible in principle, not just slow?
step.command: ./catm M2-0.c M2libc/amd64/linux/bootstrap.c M2libc/bootstrap.c M2-Planet/cc.h M2libc/bootstrappable.c M2-Planet/cc_globals.c M2-Planet/cc_reader.c M2-Planet/cc_strings.c M2-Planet/cc_types.c M2-Planet/cc_emit.c M2-Planet/cc_core.c M2-Planet/cc_macro.c M2-Planet/cc.c && ./cc_amd64 M2-0.c M2-0.M1 && ./catm M2-0-0.M1 amd64_defs.M1 libc-core.M1 M2-0.M1 && ./M0 M2-0-0.M1 M2-0.hex2 && ./catm M2-0-0.hex2 ELF-amd64.hex2 M2-0.hex2 && ./hex2-0 M2-0-0.hex2 M2

step.does: Compiles the same one-line program from the last step with your newly self-hosted M2-Planet, links it this time with the real runtime-startup file, and actually runs the result.
step.needed-for: This is the first binary in the whole ladder that gets compiled, linked, *and run*, closing the gap the last step's question pointed at: `libc-core.M1` is the piece that was missing, and this is what it does.
step.connects-to: Nothing further in this milestone, this is its real completion condition. A 229-byte seed you checksummed by hand now ends in a self-hosted compiler that produces a program the kernel will actually execute.
step.hardware: `libc-core.M1`'s own source is short and readable: set up `argv`/`envp` from the stack the kernel handed this process at exec time, call `main`, then use `main`'s own return value as the argument to the `exit` syscall. Everything between "the CPU starts executing your program" and "your `main` function runs" is these few real lines, not magic.
step.question: The exit code you're about to see should be 42. If it weren't, if `main`'s return value never made it into the exit code, which single line above would you suspect first?
step.command: ./M2 --architecture amd64 -f tiny.c -o tiny.M1 && ./catm tiny-0.M1 amd64_defs.M1 libc-core.M1 tiny.M1 && ./M0 tiny-0.M1 tiny.hex2 && ./catm tiny-0.hex2 ELF-amd64.hex2 tiny.hex2 && ./hex2-0 tiny-0.hex2 tiny && ./tiny; echo "exit code: $?"

milestone.title: Stage0: from M2-Planet to a real GCC

step.does: Compiles blood-elf's real source with the self-hosted M2-Planet from the previous milestone, in `--bootstrap-mode` (the mode M2-Planet itself needs when compiling code that pokes at raw ELF structure).
step.needed-for: blood-elf reads a compiled program and generates the symbol-table "footer" hex2 needs to resolve function names into addresses, M0 could stand in for a lot of this ladder, but from here on the real tools need blood-elf specifically, so it has to exist first.
step.connects-to: Every step from here on links through blood-elf, not straight from compiler to hex2, the ladder just grew a stage.
step.hardware: Debug symbol tables aren't optional metadata here, hex2's own two-pass label resolution (from hex1/hex2 back in `assembler`) needs *something* recording where each function starts. blood-elf builds exactly that table by walking the compiled M1 output looking for label definitions.
step.question: M2-Planet, cc_amd64's own successor, is now building tools your compiler ladder depends on going forward. What changed to make that the normal case instead of the exception?
step.command: ./M2 --architecture amd64 -f M2libc/amd64/linux/bootstrap.c -f M2libc/bootstrap.c -f M2libc/bootstrappable.c -f mescc-tools/stringify.c -f mescc-tools/blood-elf.c --bootstrap-mode -o blood-elf-0.M1 && ./catm blood-elf-0-0.M1 M2libc/amd64/amd64_defs.M1 M2libc/amd64/libc-core.M1 blood-elf-0.M1 && ./M0 blood-elf-0-0.M1 blood-elf-0.hex2 && ./catm blood-elf-0-0.hex2 M2libc/amd64/ELF-amd64.hex2 blood-elf-0.hex2 && ./hex2-0 blood-elf-0-0.hex2 blood-elf-0

step.does: Compiles M1 (the real macro assembler, a fuller, self-standing version of the M0 you built earlier) from its own C source, using M2-Planet and the blood-elf you just built. Then compiles a fuller hex2 (hex2-1) from its own C source the same way.
step.needed-for: Real M1 is a separate, more complete tool than M0, it's what the rest of this milestone (and the real Mes/TinyCC/GCC chain beyond it) actually uses to turn compiled M1-macro output into hex2 syntax. hex2-1 is the first hex2 built from real C source rather than hand-assembled hex2 syntax.
step.connects-to: These are intermediate ("-0" generation) tools, not yet self-hosted, since they were built by M2-Planet rather than by themselves. The next step closes that gap.
step.hardware: Nothing new at the hardware level, same compile/assemble/link mechanism as every prior step. What's new is *which* tool is doing which job: from here, M1 replaces M0 and hex2-1 replaces hex2-0 as the working parts of the pipeline.
step.command: ./M2 --architecture amd64 -f M2libc/amd64/linux/bootstrap.c -f M2libc/bootstrap.c -f M2libc/bootstrappable.c -f mescc-tools/stringify.c -f mescc-tools/M1-macro.c --bootstrap-mode --debug -o M1-macro-0.M1 && ./blood-elf-0 --64 --little-endian -f M1-macro-0.M1 -o M1-macro-0-footer.M1 && ./catm M1-macro-0-0.M1 M2libc/amd64/amd64_defs.M1 M2libc/amd64/libc-core.M1 M1-macro-0.M1 M1-macro-0-footer.M1 && ./M0 M1-macro-0-0.M1 M1-macro-0.hex2 && ./catm M1-macro-0-0.hex2 M2libc/amd64/ELF-amd64-debug.hex2 M1-macro-0.hex2 && ./hex2-0 M1-macro-0-0.hex2 M1-0 && ./M2 --architecture amd64 -f M2libc/sys/types.h -f M2libc/stddef.h -f M2libc/sys/utsname.h -f M2libc/amd64/linux/unistd.c -f M2libc/amd64/linux/fcntl.c -f M2libc/fcntl.c -f M2libc/amd64/linux/sys/stat.c -f M2libc/ctype.c -f M2libc/stdlib.c -f M2libc/stdarg.h -f M2libc/stdio.h -f M2libc/stdio.c -f M2libc/bootstrappable.c -f mescc-tools/hex2.h -f mescc-tools/hex2_linker.c -f mescc-tools/hex2_word.c -f mescc-tools/hex2.c --debug -o hex2_linker-1.M1 && ./blood-elf-0 --64 --little-endian -f hex2_linker-1.M1 -o hex2_linker-1-footer.M1 && ./M1-0 --architecture amd64 --little-endian -f M2libc/amd64/amd64_defs.M1 -f M2libc/amd64/libc-full.M1 -f hex2_linker-1.M1 -f hex2_linker-1-footer.M1 -o hex2_linker-1.hex2 && ./catm hex2_linker-1-0.hex2 M2libc/amd64/ELF-amd64-debug.hex2 hex2_linker-1.hex2 && ./hex2-0 hex2_linker-1-0.hex2 hex2-1

step.does: Uses M1-0 (just built) to rebuild both M1 and hex2 a second time, this time from their own real C source compiled by M2-Planet directly, producing the final, canonical `M1` and `hex2` binaries the rest of the real chain expects by name.
step.needed-for: This is the same "rebuild yourself from your own source" self-hosting pattern M2-Planet itself went through at the end of `assembler`, M1-0 exists only long enough to build the real M1.
step.connects-to: From here on, every later step calls `M1` and `hex2` directly by name, the "-0"/"-1" intermediate generations are done being needed.
step.hardware: Confirms the same thing Phase 0's hex0 self-check confirmed at the very start of this whole ladder: a tool built by an intermediate stage should be able to rebuild the real, final version of itself once the pipeline is complete enough, self-hosting isn't a one-time event at the very end, it happens at almost every stage.
step.question: M1-0 built the real M1. What would you check to convince yourself M1-0 isn't secretly needed forever, that M1, once built, can now stand fully on its own?
step.command: ./M2 --architecture amd64 -f M2libc/sys/types.h -f M2libc/stddef.h -f M2libc/amd64/linux/fcntl.c -f M2libc/fcntl.c -f M2libc/sys/utsname.h -f M2libc/amd64/linux/unistd.c -f M2libc/stdarg.h -f M2libc/string.c -f M2libc/ctype.c -f M2libc/stdlib.c -f M2libc/stdio.h -f M2libc/stdio.c -f M2libc/bootstrappable.c -f mescc-tools/stringify.c -f mescc-tools/M1-macro.c --debug -o M1-macro-1.M1 && ./blood-elf-0 --64 --little-endian -f M1-macro-1.M1 -o M1-macro-1-footer.M1 && ./M1-0 --architecture amd64 --little-endian -f M2libc/amd64/amd64_defs.M1 -f M2libc/amd64/libc-full.M1 -f M1-macro-1.M1 -f M1-macro-1-footer.M1 -o M1-macro-1.hex2 && ./hex2-1 --architecture amd64 --little-endian --base-address 0x00600000 -f M2libc/amd64/ELF-amd64-debug.hex2 -f M1-macro-1.hex2 -o M1 && ./M2 --architecture amd64 -f M2libc/sys/types.h -f M2libc/stddef.h -f M2libc/sys/utsname.h -f M2libc/amd64/linux/unistd.c -f M2libc/amd64/linux/fcntl.c -f M2libc/fcntl.c -f M2libc/amd64/linux/sys/stat.c -f M2libc/ctype.c -f M2libc/stdlib.c -f M2libc/stdarg.h -f M2libc/stdio.h -f M2libc/stdio.c -f M2libc/bootstrappable.c -f mescc-tools/hex2.h -f mescc-tools/hex2_linker.c -f mescc-tools/hex2_word.c -f mescc-tools/hex2.c --debug -o hex2_linker-2.M1 && ./blood-elf-0 --64 --little-endian -f hex2_linker-2.M1 -o hex2_linker-2-footer.M1 && ./M1 --architecture amd64 --little-endian -f M2libc/amd64/amd64_defs.M1 -f M2libc/amd64/libc-full.M1 -f hex2_linker-2.M1 -f hex2_linker-2-footer.M1 -o hex2_linker-2.hex2 && ./hex2-1 --architecture amd64 --little-endian --base-address 0x00600000 -f M2libc/amd64/ELF-amd64-debug.hex2 -f hex2_linker-2.hex2 -o hex2

step.does: Compiles a real POSIX-ish shell, `kaem`, from its own C source, with the now fully self-hosted M2-Planet, M1, and hex2, then actually runs a script through it.
step.needed-for: Every real orchestration script this whole project is built from (the ones you've been reading commands out of since `assembler` began) is a `.kaem` script, this is the tool that runs them. Real bootstrap builds stop hand-typing individual commands from here and start running scripts.
step.connects-to: The mescc-tools-extra utilities the real Mes build needs (`ungz`, `untar`, `sha256sum`...) get built and run under this same real `kaem`, not under `bash`.
step.hardware: A shell is, underneath, just a program that reads text, calls other programs, and manages exit codes, there's no special hardware mode for "being a shell." Watching a hand-built one actually parse and execute a script line makes that concrete instead of assumed.
step.command: ./M2 --architecture amd64 -f M2libc/sys/types.h -f M2libc/stddef.h -f M2libc/sys/utsname.h -f M2libc/amd64/linux/unistd.c -f M2libc/amd64/linux/fcntl.c -f M2libc/fcntl.c -f M2libc/ctype.c -f M2libc/stdlib.c -f M2libc/string.c -f M2libc/stdarg.h -f M2libc/stdio.h -f M2libc/stdio.c -f M2libc/bootstrappable.c -f mescc-tools/Kaem/kaem.h -f mescc-tools/Kaem/variable.c -f mescc-tools/Kaem/kaem_globals.c -f mescc-tools/Kaem/kaem.c --debug -o kaem.M1 && ./blood-elf-0 --64 --little-endian -f kaem.M1 -o kaem-footer.M1 && ./M1 --architecture amd64 --little-endian -f M2libc/amd64/amd64_defs.M1 -f M2libc/amd64/libc-full.M1 -f kaem.M1 -f kaem-footer.M1 -o kaem.hex2 && ./hex2 --architecture amd64 --little-endian --base-address 0x00600000 -f M2libc/amd64/ELF-amd64-debug.hex2 -f kaem.hex2 -o kaem && echo 'echo "hello from real kaem"' > test.kaem && ./kaem --verbose --strict --file test.kaem

step.does: Rebuilds blood-elf a final time and builds a new tool, `get_machine` (which detects the host's own CPU architecture), both now compiled by the self-hosted M2-Planet/M1/hex2 trio rather than the earlier bootstrap chain.
step.needed-for: M2-Mesoplanet (next step) looks for tools named exactly `M2-Planet`, `blood-elf`, `M1`, and `hex2` on its path, the earlier names (`M2`, `blood-elf-0`) were intermediate scaffolding, not what the real chain calls its tools from here on.

step.hardware: `va_start`/`va_arg` (how a C function reads its own variable arguments, like `printf`'s format-string tail) has no single, universal machine-level implementation, it depends entirely on how the calling convention actually places arguments. Mes's OWN implementation assumes a named parameter's address is literally where its value lives on the stack; GCC 14, at any optimization above `-O0`, is free to (and does) copy an unused, address-taken parameter into a different stack slot instead, since the C standard never promises otherwise.
step.question: The same construction passes at every optimization level with `__builtin_va_start` instead of the hand-rolled version, and also passes at every level if the parameter is declared `volatile`. What do both of those fixes have in common, in terms of what they force the compiler to stop assuming?

step.does: Compiles Mes's own real `_start` (the very first code this course's own original assembler ladder produces for any program) with this new GCC 14, at three different optimization levels, and checks what survives.
step.needed-for: A real, load-bearing constraint that shapes exactly how every later step in this milestone invokes this GCC: `crt1.o`, the file every program's own startup code lives in, has to be compiled at `-O0` specifically, or the resulting program segfaults immediately.
step.connects-to: Every later step that builds a C library's own startup file for this compiler (there are several, further on) follows this exact rule.
step.hardware: Mes's `_start` is written in inline assembly that reads its own arguments straight off `%ebp`, the frame-base register, a real, valid, if old-fashioned, technique. GCC 14 above `-O0` doesn't set up a frame base for a function unless something inside it needs one, and inline assembly doesn't count as "needing one" from the compiler's point of view: the register that code expects to find its data in is never populated, and the program crashes on its very first real instruction.
